papers.title_in_file: Physics-inspired Machine Learning for Quantum Error Mitigation
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section II, Section III results (QAOA-type and GHZ), Section IV conclusion; not the Methods derivations in detail or the supplementary.
papers.what_it_is: Proposes NNAS, a physics-inspired neural network for machine-learning quantum error mitigation, tested in simulated QAOA-type and GHZ circuits.

assertions.value: The authors report that NNAS reduces MAE by an average of 65.85% compared to the noisy case and by 35.12% over the best-performing QEM methods, when trained on a limited dataset of 100 sequences.
quotes: Our model significantly reduces MAE by an average of 65.85% across two key calculations compared to the noisy case (Noisy) and by 35.12% over the best-performing QEM methods
this achievement comes with training on a limited dataset of 100 sequences
assertions.certainty_reason: One simulated study on one circuit family; the authors' own comparison.
assertions.reader_inference: Numbers come from simulated six-qubit Trotterized Ising circuits, not hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report that NNAS maintains accuracy with a 90% reduction in dataset size, and achieves peak accuracy with sampling overhead reduced by 1-2 orders of magnitude compared to standard QEM methods.
quotes: its ability to maintain accuracy with a 90% reduction in dataset size
Our model achieves peak accuracy with the sampling overhead reduced by 1-2 orders of magnitude compared to standard QEM methods
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the evaluation uses six-qubit circuits with random circuit parameters, with layer depth (Trotter step) varied from 1 to 20.
quotes: We evaluate our model's performance on six-qubit circuits with random circuit parameters, varying the layer depth (Trotter step) from 1 to 20.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of evaluation scope, Section III.A, p.5
assertions.reader_inference: The six-qubit scale limits what the results say about large circuits.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section II, Section VI simulation setup and IRIS results, Section VII conclusion; not the error-analysis proofs or appendices.
papers.what_it_is: Proposes a trainable quantum feature mapping and a support-vector-based quantum SVM, with qiskit simulations on the IRIS data set.

assertions.value: The authors report average classification success rates of 92%, 91.8%, and 94.8% for r = 0, 1, and 2 respectively when 4 samples are used to prepare the ensemble model and 100 data are classified.
quotes: select 4 samples to prepare the ensemble model, then classify 100 data. The average classification success rates for r = 0, 1, and 2 are 92%, 91.8%, and 94.8%, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single small simulated study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the numerical validation targets the IRIS data set with 3 labels and 4 features and 50 samples per class, run in the Python qiskit package.
quotes: We target the IRIS data set with L = 3 labels and 4 features, and each class has 50 samples.
to validate the feasibility in Python qiskit package
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of its validation setup, Section VI.
assertions.reader_inference: Only a 150-sample classical data set in simulation; no hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that the barren plateau phenomenon during the optimization process is an open question for their method.
quotes: the barren plateau phenomenon during the optimization process, as it is an open question
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own stated limit, Section VII Conclusion and Prospect.

papers.title_in_file: The Spectral Amplitude Principle for Dynamics of Quantum Neural Networks
papers.version_note: The file is arXiv 2409.06682v3 (Dec 2025), retitled from the earlier 'Frequency principle' title in the file name; it matches the record name.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, remarks and limitations, Section 3 DNN comparison excerpt, Section 4 conclusion; proofs in Section 2 not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: Analyzes QNN training dynamics in the frequency domain with the quantum neural tangent kernel and compares QNNs to DNNs on high-frequency tasks.

assertions.value: The authors state they prove, via frequency-domain gradient and residual dynamics with the quantum neural tangent kernel, that QNN training is governed primarily by the magnitude of spectral components rather than their frequency indices.
quotes: we prove that QNN training is governed primarily by the magnitude of spectral components rather than their frequency indices
assertions.certainty_reason: Derivation within the data re-uploading QNN setting; proof steps not read by this reader.
assertions.reader_inference: Applies to data re-uploading QNNs under gradient-based training (see the stated limits).

assertions.value: The authors report that the best classical DNN configuration [200, 200, 200, 100] reached training accuracy 0.99 and testing accuracy 0.75, and that QNNs with two orders of magnitude fewer parameters show robust generalization across the entire frequency spectrum.
quotes: the configuration [200, 200, 200, 100] yields the highest training (0.99) and testing (0.75) accuracy among the classical candidates
possessing two orders of magnitude fewer parameters, the QNNs show robust generalization capabilities across the entire frequency spectrum
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation comparison from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: Classical simulation of ideal QNNs against a classical DNN sweep.

assertions.value: The authors state that their empirical validation relies on classical simulations of ideal state evolution, and that the Amplitude Priority mechanism is strictly derived from a gradient-based optimization perspective.
quotes: Our empirical validation relies on classical simulations of ideal state evolution.
the Amplitude Priority mechanism is strictly derived from a gradient-based optimization perspective
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' Remarks and Limitations paragraph, Section 1.

papers.title_in_file: AQKA: Active Quantum Kernel Acquisition Under a Shot Budget
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section 7 discussion and limitations, Section 8 conclusion, one appendix paragraph; derivations and appendices otherwise not read.
papers.what_it_is: Proposes AQKA, a sensitivity-driven shot allocation for estimating quantum kernels under a fixed measurement budget, tested in simulation and on IBM hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state that the regime picture is empirical: AQKA is the strongest allocator they tested in the budget-limited, sensitivity-concentrated regime, and a different method takes over at saturating budgets.
quotes: The regime picture is empirical: AQKA is the strongest allocator we tested in the budgetlimited, sensitivity-concentrated regime
takes over at saturating budgets, and a leverage-score AQKA variant is safer on low-Gini real data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical regime characterization from the authors' own tests.

assertions.value: The authors report that on low-Gini real data (digits 3-vs-5, 0-vs-8) AQKA is neutral to −17 pts, and that a leverage-score AQKA variant stays competitive.
quotes: On low-Gini real data (digits 3-vs-5, 0-vs-8; Appendix C.8) AQKA is neutral to −17 pts; a leverage-score AQKA variant stays competitive.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' stated limitation from their own experiments.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the Havlicek ad-hoc task the oracle full-shot kernel achieves 1.00 test accuracy under KRR, yet every shot-budgeted method plateaus near 0.60, and they attribute this to a kernel-label mismatch rather than to allocation.
quotes: Despite the oracle fullshot kernel achieving 1.00 test accuracy under both KRR
plateaus near 0.60 even at B = 106 shots
assertions.certainty_reason: One synthetic task in simulation.

papers.title_in_file: QC-Forest: a Classical-Quantum Algorithm to Provably Speedup Retraining of Random Forest
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section V entropy discussion, Section VI conclusions; algorithm details and appendices not read.
papers.what_it_is: A hybrid classical-quantum algorithm for time-efficient retraining of random forest models in a data-streaming setting, with classical numerical simulations.

assertions.value: The authors state that QC-Forest achieves a runtime poly-logarithmic in the total number of accumulated samples when retraining in the streaming setting.
quotes: achieving a runtime poly-logarithmic in the total number of accumulated samples
assertions.certainty_reason: Complexity claim under quantum-accessible data structure assumptions; proof not read by this reader.
assertions.reader_inference: Needs quantum hardware and a quantum-accessible data structure that does not exist at scale today.

assertions.value: The authors state that the initial model construction takes time linear in N, because building the quantum-accessible classical data structure is linear in N.
quotes: This is precisely the reason of why Des-q, and also our QC-Forest algorithm, take time linear in N for the initial model construction.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own stated limit, Section I.A.

assertions.value: The authors report that, using a classical implementation of the algorithm, QC-Forest achieves competitive accuracy against state-of-the-art RF methods on benchmark datasets with up to 80,000 samples.
quotes: we showcase that QC-Forest achieves competitive accuracy in comparison to state-of-the-art RF methods on widely used benchmark datasets with up to 80,000 samples
We utilize the classical implementation of the algorithm and perform extensive numerical analysis
assertions.certainty_reason: Classical simulation of the algorithm; no quantum run.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the single-tree entropy comparison QC-Forest overlaps the baseline at D = 2 but, for higher depths, the baseline is more effective in reducing the entropy.
quotes: We observe that for D = 2, QC-Forest-c manages to reduce the entropy, overlapping with the baseline.
For higher depths, the baseline method is much effective in reducing the entropy.
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical comparison.

papers.title_in_file: Robust Angle Finding for Generalized Quantum Signal Processing
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, preliminaries start, numerical results discussion, Section VII discussion; proofs in appendices not read.
papers.what_it_is: Extends generalized quantum signal processing and gives a Prony-method angle-finding algorithm, benchmarked for Hamiltonian simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Prony-based angle-finding algorithm generates angle sequences of precision 10−13 for polynomial degrees up to hundreds within a second.
quotes: successfully generates angle sequence of precision 10−13 up to polynomial degrees of hundreds within a second
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical benchmark from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report, from a numerical benchmark for Hamiltonian simulation, that the GQSP scheme essentially halves the queries to signal operators compared to ordinary QSP at precision 10−13.
quotes: we find that our scheme essentially halves the queries to signal operators compared to the ordinary QSP that can be readily applied at precision of 10−13
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors state that the optimization-based method performs poorly for GQSP, as opposed to the stable performance for ordinary QSP, and that how stable the root-finding approach is in general is an open problem.
quotes: It is crucial to mention the poor performance of the optimization-based method for GQSP, as opposed to the stable performance for the ordinary QSP.
it is an open problem how stable this approach is in general
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own stated limit in the numerical-results discussion.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section 6 conclusion, figure captions on noise; the middle sections on QUBO construction and spectra not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: A short project report encoding the Hamiltonian cycle problem for QAOA and simulating triangle and square graphs with and without noise.

assertions.value: The author states that the embedding requires (n − 1)2 qubits, so simulation is limited to n no more than 6, and that n = 3 and 4 (a triangle and a square) were simulated.
quotes: since the embedding require (n − 1)2 qubits, I can only simulate up to no more than n = 6
I choose n = 3, 4 and run the simulation on the simplest case: A triangle and a square.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author's own stated limit, Section 6 Conclusion.

assertions.value: The author reports that in the square case QAOA gave a much better result on a noisy simulator than on a noiseless one, and says the explanation requires further investigation.
quotes: However, in the square case, the result of running QAOA is much better than on a noiseless simulator!
The explanation for this phenomena require further investigation
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-author small simulation; cause not established.
assertions.reader_inference: The author gives no mechanism, so this is an unexplained simulation outcome.

assertions.value: The author reports that the Rx mixer performs much better than the Ry mixer in this problem.
quotes: It turns out that Rx mixer performs much better than Ry mixer in this problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single small simulation study.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum algorithms for hypergraph simplex finding
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sections 1.1 to 1.4 (introduction, results, open problems); preliminaries and proofs not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: Theory paper on quantum query algorithms for simplex finding in hypergraphs, with a rank-reduction theorem and a 4-simplex algorithm.

assertions.value: The paper shows that for any constant rank r, an O(nr/2) quantum algorithm for finding a simplex in rank-r hypergraphs would imply an O(n) quantum algorithm for triangle finding.
quotes: an O(nr/2) algorithm for simplex finding in rank r hypergraphs (for any specific constant r) implies an O(n) algorithm for triangle finding
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1, Section 1.2

assertions.value: The paper proves an adaptive learning graph algorithm for 4-simplex finding with O(n2.455) quantum queries, improving the trivial O(n2.5) algorithm.
quotes: There is an adaptive learning graph algorithm that computes 4-simplex finding with O(n2.455) quantum queries.
improving the trivial O(n2.5) algorithm
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 3, Section 1.2

assertions.value: The authors state that no non-trivial lower bound is known for any graph search problem.
quotes: no non-trivial lower bound is known for any graph search problem
assertions.certainty_reason: Statement about the state of knowledge, not the paper's own result.
